household: with his parents and his sister Phoebe
creator: J. D. Salinger
address_as_given: the family apartment off Fifth Avenue on East 71st Street, on the 12th or 13th floor
geocode_query: East 71st Street and Fifth Avenue, Manhattan
notes: Neither source quotes a street number from the novel. Mic places the apartment at East 71st and Fifth; a fan photo tour, reasoning from clues in the text (Phoebe crossing Fifth to the park, a high floor), picks 3 East 71st Street, which is that fan's inference.
source_quote: Holden returns to an apartment on E 71st and Fifth Avenue, where his parents await.
source2_quote: The building I focus on is 3 E. 71st

household: with his wife; Holden sleeps on their couch for part of one night
creator: J. D. Salinger
address_as_given: an apartment on Sutton Place
geocode_query: Sutton Place and East 58th Street, Manhattan
notes: Holden's former English teacher. The street is named but no building; Sutton Place runs only from East 57th to East 59th Street, so the radius is small.
source_quote: Sutton Place. Home of Mr. Antolini, a former teacher, that Holden tries to crash after leaving his parent’s apartment.

household: with her parents Silla and Deighton Boyce, her sister Ina and boarders
creator: Paule Marshall
address_as_given: a rented brownstone on Chauncey Street, Brooklyn
geocode_query: Chauncey Street and Stuyvesant Avenue, Brooklyn
notes: The novel names Chauncey Street but no number; the street runs a long way east through Bedford-Stuyvesant, so the point is a midpoint guess. Silla Boyce works to buy the house the family rents. Marshall herself grew up at 501 Hancock Street, which is not the fictional address.
source_quote: This burdensome wisdom has come to Selina from observing her family, the boarders in the house for which her mother labors and which she hopes some day to buy, and the neighbors on Chauncey Street.
source2_quote: is set in Bedford-Stuyvesant of the 1930s

household: with her father Reb Smolinsky, her mother and her sisters Bessie, Mashah and Fania
creator: Anzia Yezierska
address_as_given: Hester Street (Book I is titled "Hester Street")
geocode_query: Hester Street and Forsyth Street, Manhattan
notes: The novel names Hester Street but gives no number; the point is mid-street. Setting years are an estimate; Sara is about ten when the book opens. The family later moves to a store in Elizabeth, New Jersey, which is out of scope. Quote is from the 1925 Doubleday first edition scan (public domain).
source_quote: in such a lost corner as Hester Street lives such a fine, such a pure, silken soul as Reb Smolinsky?
source2_quote: A longing came over me for the old kitchen in Hester Street.

creator: Toni Morrison
address_as_given: an apartment building on Lenox Avenue
geocode_query: Lenox Avenue and West 130th Street, Manhattan
notes: Lenox Avenue is named but no cross street; the point is an arbitrary spot in the Harlem stretch, hence the wide radius. The couple came to Harlem from Virginia in 1906; the 1926 date is when the novel's present action takes place.
source_quote: They live in an apartment building on Lenox Avenue

creator: Mo Willems
address_as_given: Park Slope (the book is drawn over photographs of the neighborhood)
notes: The book shows no home address. The Brooklyn Public Library calls Knuffle Bunny Park Slope's most famous fictional resident and says the laundromat in the book is a few blocks from the Park Slope Library.
source_quote: The book is set and photographed in Park Slope, following toddler Trixie as she travels the neighborhood

character: Sammy Klayman (Sam Clay) and Joe Kavalier
household: Sammy with his mother Ethel and his grandmother; his cousin Joe shares his bed from 1939
work: The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay
creator: Michael Chabon
address_as_given: an apartment in a solidly lower-middle-class building on Ocean Avenue
geocode_query: Ocean Avenue and Cortelyou Road, Brooklyn
notes: Only Ocean Avenue is given, and it runs about eight kilometers from Prospect Park to Sheepshead Bay; the point is placed in its Flatbush apartment-house stretch as a guess. Joe arrives from Prague in 1939 and moves in.
source_quote: at the back of an apartment in a solidly lower-middle-class building on Ocean Avenue

work: The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay
creator: Michael Chabon
address_as_given: a secret room on the 72nd floor of the Empire State Building (the offices of Kornblum Vanishing Creams)
notes: After returning from the war Joe lives secretly in an office in the Empire State Building. The summary source is inconsistent on how long (four or five years); years here are approximate.
source_quote: He lives in a secret room on the 72nd floor of the Empire State Building for five years

creator: Jonathan Lethem
address_as_given: an apartment above the L&L car-service storefront on Bergen Street
geocode_query: Bergen Street and Smith Street, Brooklyn
notes: LitCharts places Lionel's apartment above the L&L storefront; Wikipedia places the novel on Bergen Street between Smith and Hoyt. Combining the two is this record's inference; no number is given. The 2019 film moved the story to the 1950s and is not covered here.
source_quote: Seminole abandons Lionel, who returns home to his apartment above the L&L storefront.
source2_quote: a crime mystery set on Bergen Street between Smith and Hoyt streets

household: the families in the housing project of the book's last section
creator: Hubert Selby Jr.
address_as_given: a housing project (identified by the source as the Red Hook Houses)
notes: Bklynr identifies the project in "Landsend" as the Red Hook Houses; the rest of the book is set around 57th Street and Second Avenue in what is now Sunset Park, mostly in bars, a diner and a strike office rather than homes. Setting years are an estimate. The Red Hook Houses are a large complex, so the radius covers it.
source_quote: Selby’s six stories (save one, set in the Red Hook Houses, a public housing complex built in 1938) take place in a southwestern industrial section of the book’s titular borough

creator: James Baldwin
address_as_given: his address on Bank Street; "the hovel on Bank Street"
geocode_query: Bank Street and Bleecker Street, Manhattan
notes: Quoted from "Any Day Now," a chapter of the novel published in Partisan Review in 1960. Bank Street is named, no number. Rufus Scott's own apartment in the same passage is only described as in a warehouse district near the river, too vague to map.
source_quote: Vivaldo gave the driver his address on Bank Street and watched the taxi roll away.
source2_quote: Yet he had no home here-the hovel on Bank Street was not a home.

creator: Jay McInerney
address_as_given: a too-expensive apartment on West 12th Street
geocode_query: West 12th Street and Seventh Avenue, Manhattan
notes: The street comes from a history blog, not checked against the novel's text; no number is given and West 12th Street is long, so the radius is wide.
source_quote: a too-expensive apartment on West 12th Street (although well-appointed by his erstwhile wife)

creator: Mark Helprin
address_as_given: a hideout in the ceiling of Grand Central
notes: Peter Lake, a burglar, lives hidden behind the star ceiling of Grand Central's main concourse. The novel's early part is set in a fabulist Belle Epoque New York; years are an estimate.
source_quote: One night he mounts the horse in a stable and retires to his hideout in the ceiling of Grand Central Station.
source2_quote: Peter will later hide up behind the stars set into the ceiling of Grand Central Station

household: with her father Isaac Penn and family
creator: Mark Helprin
address_as_given: a fortress-like mansion on the Upper West Side
notes: Peter Lake breaks into the Penn house and finds Beverly at home. The family also has an estate upstate at the Lake of the Coheeries, which is outside the five boroughs and not mapped.
source_quote: attempts to rob a fortress-like mansion on the Upper West Side. Though he thinks it is empty, the daughter of the house is home.

household: with his parents Rose and Dave and his brother Donald
creator: E. L. Doctorow
address_as_given: the family's Bronx apartment, at the same street address as Doctorow's own boyhood home on Eastburn Avenue
geocode_query: Eastburn Avenue and East 173rd Street, Bronx
notes: EBSCO says the novel gives the Altschulers the Doctorows' actual street address; NYU's archive says Doctorow grew up on Eastburn Avenue. The number itself was not found in a fetchable source, so this is graded block_inferred. Late in the book the family moves to a much smaller apartment, location not sourced.
source_quote: By making the street address and first names of the fictional Altschulers coincide with the actual address
source2_quote: he grew up on Eastburn Avenue in the Bronx

creator: E. L. Doctorow
address_as_given: the Bronx's Bathgate Avenue
geocode_query: Bathgate Avenue and East 177th Street, Bronx
notes: Sources disagree slightly: Library Journal (via LitLovers) says he grew up on Bathgate Avenue, while Time says the street he took his alias from was a few blocks from his birthplace. Either way the home is in the blocks around the Bathgate Avenue market; no number given.
source_quote: Having grown up poor but ambitious on the Bronx's Bathgate Avenue during the Depression
source2_quote: Billy is his real name, Bathgate an alias he has invented, lifted from a street, known for its open-air markets, a few blocks from his birthplace in the Bronx.

source2_quote: is living with her parents on the Upper West Side

creator: Teju Cole
address_as_given: Morningside Heights, the starting point for his evening walks
notes: The novel opens with Julius setting out on walks from Morningside Heights; no street is given. Reviews say he lives uptown near Columbia.

creator: Saul Bellow
address_as_given: the Hotel Gloriana, on Broadway in the Seventies, a few blocks from the Ansonia
notes: The Gloriana is fictional. Wilhelm comes down from the twenty-third floor; the hotel newsman sees the Ansonia several blocks away, which puts it on upper Broadway near the 70s. Quote is from the novella as first printed in Partisan Review, 1956.
source_quote: Most of the guests at the Hotel Gloriana were people past the age of retirement. Along Broadway in the Seventies, Eighties and Nineties, a great part of New York's vast population of old men and women lives.
source2_quote: He came from the twenty-third floor down to the lobby on the mezzanine to collect his mail before breakfast

household: with his mother; his grandmother lives in the building across the street

address_as_given: the Upper West Side
notes: Only the neighborhood is sourced. A 2011 film-locations site lists a building at West 98th Street for the film's apartment; that is the film, not the novel, and is not mapped here.
